summary: A 1969 list of questions about the Host-IMP protocol, such as how long a link can sit idle in a time-sharing setting and whether a host rather than its IMP should control ready-for-next-message replies. It points to the network contractor's report and asks for clarification.

eli5.summary: Someone read the rules for connecting a computer to the network and wrote down what was confusing, like asking the teacher questions after reading the instructions.

questions: what are rfnm messages in the arpanet
subtitle: Questions about the Host-IMP protocol design, with responses from the ARPANET designers.

tldr.problem: John Kreznar identified potential issues in the Host-IMP protocol specification from BBN, including automatic link deletion, RFNM (ready-for-next-message) handling, and inconsistencies between different parts of the spec.
tldr.mechanism: Kreznar documents four specific concerns and asks for clarification. Bob Kahn responds with detailed explanations of the protocol design rationale, showing how link management, RFNM timing, and error handling actually work together.
tldr.outcome: This exchange of questions and answers clarifies the early protocol design and shows how the ARPANET community resolved technical disagreements through discussion and documentation.

today: This RFC is a historical record of ARPANET protocol design. The Host-IMP protocol it discusses was superseded by later standards, but the dialogue exemplifies the collaborative engineering approach that built the early Internet.

sections.title: Kreznar's Concerns
sections.content: John Kreznar raises four questions: First, automatic link deletion after 15 seconds of non-use seems bad for time-sharing systems where a human user might not send anything for minutes. Second, he asks who controls RFNM replies: does the IMP send them immediately or does the Host decide? Third, why need a special NOP message if hosts must already be prepared to retry? Fourth, how do 'arbitrary delays' in the Host software fit with automatic link deletion?
sections.eli5: If the network closes a line after 15 seconds with no traffic, what happens when someone walks away from their terminal for coffee?

sections.title: Kahn's Answers
sections.content: Bob Kahn explains that link deletion does not affect transmission: a Host sending on a deleted link entry just re-enters it in the table. No dummy messages are needed because links are 'effectively always open'. RFNMs come from the destination IMP when a message reaches the head of the output queue, protecting message order. The NOP message is for startup synchronization only, not for keeping links alive. Arbitrary host delays do not conflict with link deletion because links are only deleted when not blocked by active transmission.
sections.eli5: The network is smarter than it looks. A link is never really closed, just marked as unused. When you send again, it auto-reopens. This solves all the problems Kreznar worried about.

sections.title: Historical Significance
sections.content: This RFC and its paired response (RFC 17a) show how the ARPANET community resolved design questions through written dialogue. Rather than simply publishing a spec, the engineers documented concerns and responded with reasoned explanations. This exchange helped validate the Host-IMP protocol design and set a pattern for open technical discussion that has remained central to Internet standards.
sections.eli5: This is how engineers make sure their designs actually work: someone asks hard questions, someone else explains carefully, and everyone learns something.
